strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: existing metrics for visual brain decoding are shown to be poorly aligned with human semantic judgments, which is convincingly illustrated with concrete failure examples.

Solid empirical methodology for meta-evaluation, using multiple complementary statistics (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson correlation) against a reasonably sized human-annotated dataset (1,000 pairs, 22 raters).
The proposed sub-metrics (Object F1, Cap-Sim) are interpretable and grounded in intuitive notions of object presence and caption similarity, differing from prior black-box embedding-based metrics.

Thorough ablation and analysis: combination heatmap (Fig. 3) showing SEED's components are complementary, worst-case judgment analysis explaining why each component sometimes fails, and the EffNet extremity analysis (Table 2) is a nice diagnostic insight.
The semantic near-miss phenomenon analysis is a useful and novel characterization of a systematic failure mode of current SOTA decoding models, going beyond simply proposing a new metric.

The proposed pairwise hinge loss is shown to be compatible with and tested across three different decoding architectures (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain), demonstrating some generality of the contribution.
Commitment to open-source the human judgment data is valuable to the community and enables further metric research.
Comprehensive supplementary material including additional qualitative examples, category lists, and ablations (e.g., incorporating size/location/number information into Object F1).
weaknesses: The core human-evaluation dataset is derived from a single decoding model (MindEye2) reconstructions only; it is unclear whether SEED's superior alignment generalizes to reconstructions from qualitatively different architectures (e.g., GAN-based or older models with different failure modes).

The gains of SEED over its best single component (EffNet) are relatively modest in absolute terms (81.0% vs 78.0% pairwise accuracy; 0.621 vs 0.559 Kendall's Tau), raising the question of how much added value SEED provides beyond simply using EffNet with awareness of its known biases.

The improvements from the pairwise hinge loss are numerically small for some baselines (e.g., MindEye2 SEED improves only from .474 to .475), which weakens the claimed "consistent improvement" narrative, especially since some metrics (e.g., PixCorr, SSIM) even slightly degrade for MindEye2 and MindBridge.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals or bootstrap tests) is reported for the meta-evaluation correlations or the loss-ablation results, making it hard to assess whether observed differences are meaningful or within noise.

Object F1 is restricted to a fixed 82-category vocabulary (COCO + 2 extra), which may limit its applicability to images with objects outside this set and could bias evaluation toward COCO-like scenes.

SEED and its sub-components rely on multiple pretrained models (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer, EffNet), which could introduce compounding biases or errors from each component that are not fully explored (e.g., how caption model quality affects Cap-Sim reliability).

The MTurk annotation setup (extremely low pay of $0.03 per pair) raises potential concerns about annotation quality/care despite the stated "Master" worker filter, and inter-annotator agreement statistics are not reported in the main text.

The evaluation is limited to a single dataset (NSD/MS-COCO derived), so generalizability of both the metric and the loss improvements to other brain-decoding datasets or imaging modalities is untested.

SEED explicitly does not capture perceptual/style aspects (acknowledged as a limitation), which could be important for a complete evaluation of decoding quality, potentially limiting its standalone utility as a single go-to metric.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: current visual brain decoding evaluation metrics (PixCorr, SSIM, AlexNet, Inception, CLIP, etc.) show poor alignment with human semantic judgments despite being used ubiquitously in the field, and the paper convincingly demonstrates this gap.

Solid human evaluation methodology: 1,000 GT-reconstruction pairs rated by 22 MTurk Master workers with high inter-rater agreement (ICC=0.84), and the data is planned to be released for future research.

The proposed metric is well-motivated by neuroscience literature (two-stage visual attention theory), giving a principled rationale for combining object-level (Object F1) and caption-level (Cap-Sim) semantic representations with a global feature-based metric (EffNet).

Comprehensive meta-evaluation using three standard correlation measures (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson) plus bootstrap-based statistical significance testing showing SEED's improvement over the best baseline (EffNet) is significant.

Good robustness analyses: a second, independent human evaluation on a different dataset/model (GOD/Mind-Vis) confirms generalization, and substituting different off-the-shelf detectors/captioners/text encoders shows the framework is not overly sensitive to specific model choices.

Thorough ablation studies (Appendix C.1, C.3) systematically justify design choices, e.g., showing that adding location/size/number weighting to Object F1 does not help, and that all pairwise combinations of existing metrics underperform combinations involving the new components.

Valuable qualitative failure-mode analysis (semantic near-miss phenomenon, object-captured-but-details-missed) that provides actionable insight for future decoding model design, going beyond simply proposing a metric.
Extensive appendix material with worst-case judgment case studies that transparently discuss where SEED and its components can still fail, improving trustworthiness of the claims.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat limited: SEED is an unweighted average of three existing/simple techniques (open-vocabulary detection F1, caption similarity via off-the-shelf captioner+sentence encoder, and EfficientNet correlation), rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach; the two-stage attention framing feels like post-hoc motivation for a fairly straightforward ensemble.

The secondary human-evaluation robustness check (GOD/Mind-Vis) is quite small (only 50 image pairs, 10 student raters), limiting confidence that the alignment result generalizes across the diversity of datasets and decoding architectures used in the field.

No comparison against strong, more recent holistic judge baselines such as prompting a large multimodal/vision-language model (e.g., GPT-4V-style judge or CLIP-based VQAScore variants beyond the BLIP/GIT VQAScore reported) as an alternative semantic similarity metric, which could be a more directly competitive approach to benchmark against.

The combination weights in SEED (simple 1/3 average) are not learned or optimized against the human data despite having access to it; a learned combination might yield stronger and more principled alignment, and the paper does not explore or justify why an unweighted average is preferable beyond empirical convenience.

SEED inherits systematic biases and failure modes from its constituent off-the-shelf models (as acknowledged in Sec. 6 and Appendix D.2), and because all three components can fail simultaneously on distorted/out-of-distribution reconstructions, the metric's reliability under such realistic decoding-model failure cases is not rigorously quantified beyond a few case studies.

The magnitude of improvement over EffNet alone, while statistically significant, is often modest in absolute terms (e.g., Table 2 GOD dataset: SEED 73.7% vs EffNet 72.5% pairwise accuracy), raising questions about the practical significance of the added complexity of a three-component ensemble versus using EffNet with minor adjustments.

strengths: Addresses a real and important gap: current visual brain decoding metrics show near-perfect scores on SOTA models, hiding severe semantic failures, and the paper provides compelling motivating examples (Fig. 1) and worst-case analysis to substantiate this claim.

Rigorous human evaluation methodology: 22 MTurk Master-qualified raters on 1,000 GT-reconstruction pairs with high inter-rater agreement (ICC=0.84), plus a second independent human study on a different dataset/model (GOD/Mind-Vis) for generalization checking.

Thorough meta-evaluation using three complementary statistics (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson correlation) and statistically validated improvement of SEED over the best baseline (EffNet) via bootstrapped confidence intervals.

Extensive robustness analyses: swapping underlying off-the-shelf models (grounding, captioning, text encoding) shows minimal performance variation; ablations over all possible metric sub-combinations (Fig. 8, Tab. 5) justify the specific choice of Object F1 + Cap-Sim + EffNet.

Insightful qualitative failure-mode analysis (semantic near-miss phenomenon, object-captured-but-details-missed) that provides actionable, quantified diagnostic value for the decoding research community, applied consistently across five SOTA models.
Open release of code and, notably, the human evaluation dataset itself, which is a valuable resource enabling future metric development beyond this paper's own proposal.
Honest and detailed limitations section with concrete failure case analysis (Fig. 10, Sec. D.2) showing where SEED itself fails, adding credibility rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat modest: SEED is essentially an average of an existing metric (EffNet) with two conceptually simple new components (open-vocabulary object F1 and captioning-based cosine similarity); the neuroscientific two-stage attention framing feels like a post-hoc narrative rather than a principled design driver.

The absolute improvement of SEED over the strongest single baseline (EffNet) is statistically significant but numerically modest (e.g., Pearson 0.813 vs 0.748 on NSD, 0.706 vs 0.661 on GOD), raising the question of how large a practical difference this represents for downstream model comparison/ranking.

Object F1 relies on a fixed, closed set of 82 COCO-derived categories, which is shown in the paper's own failure analysis (e.g., 'sink' vs 'toilet' being treated as entirely mismatched) to miss synonymous/related objects; the VLM-based open-vocabulary alternative underperforms, suggesting the category-list dependency is a real limitation not fully resolved.

Human evaluation, while carefully collected, is based on a single Likert-scale semantic rating per model per dataset combination (main experiment centers on one decoding model, MindEye2, for the large-scale study; the second dataset study uses only 10 raters and 50 images), which is a relatively narrow empirical base for establishing generalizability of a proposed community-standard metric.

The paper does not benchmark against other plausible modern semantic-similarity alternatives beyond BLIP/GIT VQAScore (e.g., more recent MLLM-as-judge approaches, CLIP variants, DINO-based similarity), leaving open whether even simpler recent approaches might match or exceed SEED's alignment with humans.

The failure-mode discovery section (Sec. 5.4) is primarily descriptive/qualitative and does not propose or validate any concrete remedies, somewhat limiting the paper's contribution to diagnosis rather than actionable improvement of decoding models.

Threshold-based design choices (e.g., Object F1 > 0.7 and Object F1 - SEED > 0.2 for 'semantic detail miss' detection) are acknowledged as arbitrary, which slightly weakens the quantitative claims about failure mode prevalence rates.
